newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia tax-free feud seen behind hockey boss death.
newsitem.headline: Russia tax-free feud seen behind hockey boss death.

text.p: The murder of the head of Russia's Ice Hockey Federation has sent shockwaves through the sports establishment and prompted speculation on Wednesday about whether cash was involved in the "murder of the year".

Valentin Sych, 60, the head of the Federation and the third most influential man in Russia's sports hierarchy, was shot dead on Tuesday morning in an apparent contract killing near his country home by an unidentified attacker. His wife was wounded.

There was no comment from police on the reasons for the killing, but most Russian newspapers said the murder was likely to be a new twist in a bloody saga involving tax-free export-import activities by social organisations.
The Russian Ice Hockey Federation (RIHF) was among many organisations given tax privileges in the early 1990's to allow them to stay afloat amid a severe shortage of government funds.

The newspapers said RIHF had made extensive use of the privileges, which were scrapped last year because the government feared they were harming its own revenue-raising ability and attracting organised crime.

The Sevodnya daily said the RIHF had imported $4.2 million-worth of tobacco in 1995 and more than $20 million of hard liquor. The Izvestia newspaper said its debts to contractors after the scrapping amounted to millions of dollars.

Sevodnya said Sych, known in Russia and abroad as a highly influential figure in the hockey world, had tried to stay away from the tax-free business, but would have been a key witness in any investigation as he had to sign all documents.
"He must have been involved in commercial activities, but all the money the federation made, Sych used to support hockey," said a sports official who declined to be named.

Sych told Reuters in an interview two months ago that criminal activity in Russian sports was getting worse and that many players and officials were scared by organised crime and faced pressure to aid illegal ventures.
Media reports said police questioned officials of the RIHF's commercial branch on Tuesday night.

Newspapers and sports officials described Sych, who was the driving force in the first contacts between the Soviet Army hockey machine and the National Hockey League, as a man who had plunged his whole life into hockey and who would do anything for it, including raising funds by all possible means.

"For the benefit of Russian hockey, if I know that it is good for hockey, I will sign any document whatsoever," Sych said on an archive tape shown by Russia's NTV television, which dubbed the case "the murder of the year".
Five years of transition to a market economy have channelled vast resources into private hands and generated a spate of contract killings of businessmen, bankers and officials.
Numerous organisations enjoying the tax-free regime and tax breaks, such as the Afghan War Invalid's Foundation, were set up as charities and backed by the state.
But they soon became prime targets for criminals who used them to launder money and send it out of the country.
The National Sports Fund, which at one point handled half Russia's alcohol imports and assets running into billions of dollars, was the biggest beneficiary of the customs loophole.

Izvestia newspaper quoted Vice-President of the National Sports Fund, Boris Fyodorov, as saying Sych's murder, a bloody cemetery bombing last year and an attempt on his own life were all part of a fight over the spoils of the tax privileges.

Fyodorov narrowly escaped an assasination attempt last summer by a killer who left him with a bullet and stab wounds, but survived and accused Kremlin aides of siphoning cash out of the state-run fund, which he then headed.

A bomb blast in a Moscow cemetery last November killed 13 mourners gathered at the gravesite of the head of Afghan War Invalids' Foundation. Most of the mourners were also involved in the charity's commercial activities.
Links between crime and sport in Russia range from much rumoured but seldom proved match-rigging to strongarm attempts to take over control of sports clubs and organisations.
For 20 years up to 1989 Sych was on the Soviet Sports Committee, becoming deputy head in 1984. He became president of the Hockey Federation in 1994.

Mikhail Govorkov, a federation spokesman, said the killing was one of the factors behind the poor performance of the Russian squad in a friendly against Finland. Russia lost 1:7 ahead of the April 26 start of World Championship in Helsinki.
